extracted.intended_audience: beginning TeX users and document authors learning Plain TeX
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines and conventions for producing well-formed Plain TeX manuscripts: choosing and switching fonts, grouping, running TeX, handling hyphenation/line-breaking, and diagnosing overfull/underfull boxes. Emphasizes idiomatic usage and common pitfalls for authors preparing documents with TeX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use grouping ({...}) to confine font and definition changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Font changes and definitions made inside a group do not affect the text outside the group; grouping provides local block structure so temporary changes won't mess up the rest of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Prefer { f bold} or {	t { f ...}} style with braces rather than repeatedly typing m to restore roman; use grouping for local changes and to avoid having to remember to revert settings. Example: {	enrm smaller 
inerm and smaller} demonstrates grouping's effect on size. Avoid leaving groups unclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italic correction (\/ ) when switching from italic/slanted to unslanted text
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert the special control sequence '\/ ' just before switching back from slanted or italic to roman or bold so that the preceding letter gains an italic correction and the white space looks correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb: use \/ before switching from slanted/italic to roman/bold unless the next character is a period or comma. Examples: {	{italics\/} for {	{emphasis}}}, and to typeset a bold 'f' in quotes use { f f\/} to avoid incorrect spacing. Note that the correction amount depends on the preceding letter (e.g., more for 'f' than 'c').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer roman type for sustained reading; use special faces sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Special fonts (bold, slanted, italic, typewriter) are effective for emphasis but are tiring for sustained reading, so roman should account for the bulk of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not set long portions entirely in bold/slanted/italic; reserve such faces for emphasis or short elements (titles, headings, examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Braces and empty groups stop space absorption after control sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A trailing group '}' or an empty group '{}' can prevent TeX from absorbing an optional space after a control sequence and is useful to delimit control-sequence names or to stop space gobbling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples: use {
\TeX} or \TeX{} to ensure correct spacing after \TeX without wrongly inserting or deleting spaces. Using {} is safe in all cases where a following space might be eaten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand control-sequence behavior: 'applies to next item' vs 'change current state'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some control sequences (e.g., \centerline) apply only to the next thing that follows (and thus require braces to enclose multiword arguments), while others (e.g., \it) change the current state and affect everything that follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
When centering multiple words use \centerline{...}; to change font locally use {
\it ...}. Misplacing braces leads to different effects—learn which primitives look ahead and which don't.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties (~) to prevent line breaks between tokens that must stay together
rubrics_metrics.description: The '~' character is a tie: it acts like a normal space but prevents TeX from breaking the line at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ties in names and between initials (e.g., R.~J. Drofnats) to prevent undesirable line breaks. Useful for keeping numbers and units together or words that must not be separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use '%' to terminate a line without introducing a space (comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A '%' at the input line ends the line for TeX and causes TeX to ignore everything after it up to the line end; no blank space is inserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '%' to insert comments for human readers, or to fix spacing errors caused by end-of-line characters. Example: 'he preferred to be called---% error has been fixed!' fixes an unintended space/newline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphs are delimited by blank lines; line breaks inside paragraphs are treated as spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A blank input line tells TeX that the paragraph ended; otherwise, newlines are equivalent to spaces within a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You needn't worry about manual line breaks—TeX will reflow text. Use blank lines intentionally to start new paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation policy: TeX hyphenates as a last resort; provide discretionary hyphens or \hyphenation to assist
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX will hyphenate words only if necessary when line-breaking. Authors can give hints using discretionary hyphens (e.g., gal\-axy) or a global \hyphenation{list} at the start of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If TeX fails to find useful hyphenation points for narrow measures, insert discretionary hyphens or list hyphenations globally to improve line-breaking. See Appendix H for the hyphenation algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and act on overfull \hbox messages shown in the log
rubrics_metrics.description: When lines cannot meet spacing tolerances they produce 'Overfull \hbox' warnings; the log shows the amount too wide, abbreviated box contents, and the input location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect the .log/.transcript to find offending paragraphs (e.g., 'Overfull \hbox (0.98807pt too wide) in paragraph at lines 7--11'). The DVI/hardcopy will show a black bar; use the provided location, box contents, and amount to diagnose and fix the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Badness and tolerance control line quality; plain TeX restricts badness to 200 by default
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX assigns a numerical 'badness' to each line describing spacing quality (0 perfect; 1000 awful); plain TeX normally disallows badness above 200. When you need tighter/wider tolerances you can change \tolerance, or else rewrite the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very narrow columns (e.g., 2in) plain TeX's tolerances are inappropriate—either loosen tolerance or rewrite the copy. Badness examples: 0 perfect, 100 very tight, 200 loose, 1000 bad. Use \hbadness/\tolerance adjustments cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: For extremely narrow columns, prefer rewriting copy over forcing tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain column widths (like 2in) may be impossible without excessive spacing; loosening tolerances can hide the problem but rewriting the text to fit is often better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many Overfull/Underfull boxes occur for a column width, consider editing the text or changing layout rather than accepting poor spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \hsize to set the horizontal measure (column width)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primitive \hsize specifies the width of normal lines when TeX sets paragraphs and can be changed before inputting a file to typeset content at different widths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \hsize=4in \input story to set a 4-inch column. Experimentation with \hsize reveals overfull/underfull issues for narrow measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect the transcript/log files for diagnostic information (overfull boxes, glue/kern lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX writes a transcript/log that records warnings and detailed diagnostics (abbreviated box contents, glue/kern descriptions) useful for debugging spacing and line-break issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open story.log or texput.log to examine the exact messages TeX emitted (locations, hyphenation attempts, glue/kern listings). These are essential for advanced diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Load fonts with \font\cs=externalname at desired size or scaled factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \font\cs=externalfontname or with 'at' or 'scaled' to bring fonts into TeX's memory and associate them with control sequences (e.g., \font\ninerm=cmr9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \font\magnifiedfiverm=cmr5 at 10pt loads 5-point font magnified to 10pt. Check that your typesetter supports the scaled size; TeX will accept many sizes numerically but output may be wrong if device lacks that scaled font.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer small scale changes; design size matters—cmr10 differs from cmr5 at 10pt
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-designed font has differing shapes at different design sizes; magnifying a small-design font to a larger size is not equivalent to using a font designed for that larger size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually scale fonts only slightly relative to their design size unless post-processing (photographic reduction) is planned or an unusual effect is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scale shortcuts (\magstep, \magstephalf) for common magnifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides \magstep0, \magstep1, \magstep2, ... and \magstephalf for common geometric scale factors (1.2, 1.44, etc.) so fonts and document magnification can compose predictably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \font\bigtenrm=cmr10 scaled\magstep2; document-level \magnification combines with font-scale in predictable ways (scales add multiplicatively as magsteps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \global to make assignments persist beyond the current group
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition or assignment prefixed with \global applies to all existing groups (not just the innermost), making changes permanent across group boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \global\advance\count0 by 1 inside an output routine will increment the page number persistently. Use \global when you want side effects to survive group termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \begingroup and \endgroup for block structure across control sequences; groups must be properly nested
rubrics_metrics.description: Begingroup/endgroup primitives let you start a group in one control sequence and end it in another. After macro expansion, the resulting grouping must be properly nested (no overlapping groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not produce overlapping groups (e.g., '{ \begingroup } \endgroup' is illegal). Consider implementing named block macros (\beginthe{name} / \endthe{name}) cautiously and ensure nesting discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the initial TeX prompt behavior and format preloading
rubrics_metrics.description: On startup TeX prompts with '**' to ask for a file name; if the first character after '**' is not '\\' TeX automatically inserts '\\input'. If the first char is '&' TeX replaces memory with a precomputed format before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may also invoke TeX as 'tex story' from the shell. Use '&plain story' to load the plain format before inputting the file when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that some typographic conventions are changing (italic semicolons, slanted vs italic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Older style guides recommend punctuation after a word be in the same font; modern practice sometimes prefers punctuation in roman even when preceding word is italic; slanted roman can be preferable for certain uses (titles, bibliographies) and avoid confusion with math italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of typographic choice tradeoffs; slanted type is often used to distinguish from math italics and for titles. The manual notes evolving conventions—choose consistently and for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overuse font-size switching—only when there is good reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive switching among sizes and faces is visually distracting and generally unnecessary in ordinary manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Font-size variations (e.g., for 'poetic' effects) are acceptable occasionally, but avoid frequent arbitrary switching unless there is a substantive typographic reason.
